Last Friday, I was in Millinocket as we cut the ribbon on Millinocket Regional Hospital’s new emergency department. It was great to meet with hospital staff and supporters and tour the new state-of-the-art facility. As a native of Caribou, I know how important emergency health care access is to the vitality, and even the survival, of our state’s rural communities.

Seeing the beautiful new emergency department in Millinocket, I was struck by how thoughtfully it was designed and built to meet the specific needs of this region. This critical addition to the community will help increase access to quality emergency services for both residents and visitors of the Katahdin Region alike.

It was a pleasure to congratulate the leaders, staff, and supporters of Millinocket Regional Hospital on this important advancement, and I was proud to help make it possible by securing nearly $13.4 million through my role on the Senate Appropriations Committee to support the construction this facility, which has doubled the number of ER rooms available to patients.

I am saddened to learn of the passing of Andrew Cross, the volunteer firefighter who lost his life while responding to the fire at Robbins Lumber in Searsmont yesterday. My heart goes out to his family, his friends, and the Morrill Volunteer Fire Department, where he served.

A member of my staff knew Andrew for many years and played soccer with him from the time they were young. He said that everyone knew Andrew as a kindhearted, hardworking Maine man who loved his family, his dogs, and the people of his community. He was the kind of person who could always be seen with a smile on his face, and his loss is being felt deeply.

Andrew’s life is a shining example of the courage, bravery, and selfless love of others that can be found in every town and city across our great state. Our first responders give more than we could ever repay to help keep us and our loved ones safe, and it is incumbent on us to honor their sacrifices. May Andrew’s memory be a blessing.

The Robbins family is beloved in the Searsmont community, and Robbins Lumber is a piece of Maine history. I have known the family for many years. My heart goes out to them, their employees, and the first responders who have come from all over the region to help in the emergency response. This is a very sad crisis, and all those affected are in my prayers.

It cuts programs that help us diversify our energy supply chain and make sure that America stays on the cutting edge of research and development, it undermines nuclear security, and it abandons communities dealing with nuclear contamination from past defense projects. As a result, American families and businesses are going to face higher fuel and utility costs and many communities will be left less safe.

During the debate, I tried to improve the bill by supporting an amendment that would increase the critical minerals and energy innovation fund and restore the electricity account. This would help make America more energy independent, maintain the electrical grid and help make sure it is reliable, and ensure that we are not relying on foreign adversaries for materials vital to manufacturing and technology that drive our economy.

The amendment would help make sure that American families can afford to keep the lights on, farmers can operate, and local businesses can continue to function.

You can also watch my opening remarks here:
https://youtu.be/dgZteJue-fs

1. Trump sued his own government for $10B over an IRS leak involving thousands of other people. He was effectively both the plaintiff and the defendant in the case.

2. IRS lawyers prepared a memo outlining the weakness of Trump’s lawsuit and recommending the DOJ seek dismissal, not to settle.

3. Instead, Trump dropped the lawsuit. In exchange, the DOJ created a $1.8 billion “anti-weaponization” fund for political allies claiming they were targeted by the federal government —January 6 rioters that attacked cops, election deniers, members of Congress, right wing influencers. 

4. The cash would be distributed by a commission appointed by Trump’s Attorney General — while Trump retains the authority to remove those members, giving him enormous influence over where the money ultimately goes.

5. That’s not all! As part of the agreement, the IRS would halt audits involving Trump, his family, and related entities. An audit dispute regarding Trump’s Chicago tower would have cost Trump $100M+ if the IRS prevailed. That’s erased under this deal.

It seems like this looting of the government by Trump, his family, and his allies may be too blatantly corrupt for even some Republicans to stomach, as some are starting to oppose it. 

Sadly, this is just another chapter in Trump using the presidency to enrich himself off the backs of American taxpayers. 

We must put an end to this. 
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/05/19/admin/irs-trump-lawsuit-deal.html?unlocked_article_code=1.j1A.yiyd.PwJCpsH17y-N&smid=url-share

In July of 2024, while President Trump was campaigning in Butler, Pennsylvania, a gunman fired at the President. As the bullet grazed his ear on live television, I, as well as most Americans, were left in a state of disbelief and shock. This attempted assassination was chilling. It was a horrific attack of democracy and was just simply un-American.

This was an event I hoped our nation would never experience again. Yet, just two months later, authorities reported another attempted assassination of the President. In September of 2024, a man was spotted hiding in the bushes with a rifle aiming at the golf course where President Trump was golfing in Florida. Luckily, a Secret Service agent engaged the suspect before President Trump came into the shooter’s view. Nonetheless, it was another attempted attack on our President and, therefore, our nation.

Then, this weekend, a gunman with multiple weapons stormed the event venue of the White House Correspondents Dinner. Shots were fired, one of our brave Secret Service agents was hit, and the attacker left behind a manifesto claiming all Trump Administration officials, excluding one, were his targets. Luckily, no one was injured. However, the fact of the matter is this: this is the third time in less than two years that President Trump has faced an assassination attempt.

This should make every American, regardless of their political views, stop and reflect on the condition of our current culture and why this is happening.

Political violence is never acceptable – and I truly do believe the majority of Americans instinctively reject political violence. Most of us know what happened on Saturday night is wrong. Yet, as we reflect on this horrific event, we ought to think about what this political violence represents. To me, it symbolizes a deeper problem within our own society, culture, and political system.

Political rhetoric in our country has gotten out of hand. I am not naïve. I know that reckless rhetoric is not a tactic used by just one political party. However, today, I am speaking about the three assassination attempts on President Trump.

When I hear politicians compare the President to Hitler or compare federal law enforcement agencies like Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Border Patrol to Nazi Germany’s Gestapo and SS, I am appalled. Anyone who has read the history books knows how false and out of touch with reality those comparisons are. Moreover, it should be obvious that such rhetoric is dangerous. In fact, this kind of rhetoric is exactly what fuels the unstable and violence prone members of our society to act.

So, while I do think there will be almost a universal rejection by elected officials of the violence that occurred at the event on Saturday, I encourage all elected officials to think more deeply. I encourage them to stop and look at their own rhetoric when speaking about the President and their other political opponents. If that language is provocative, they ought to correct it immediately. Furthermore, I urge all American citizens to condemn politicians – from either party – who use problematic language when talking about the President, federal agencies, or other politicians. Dangerous rhetoric must end immediately.

The second thing we ought to remember is that many of the law enforcement officials who bravely and swiftly acted to protect the President, Vice President, our Cabinet members, and many of my colleagues on Saturday night are currently operating under an agency that is not funded. The events at the White House Correspondents Dinner this weekend demonstrate just how unacceptable it is to fail to fund the government, particularly the Department of Homeland Security, during this time of threats from abroad and political turmoil at home.

It is a huge mistake not to fund DHS and the selfless law enforcement agents who work within that agency. We should never, ever close an agency that protects not just the President, but every American citizen. It is unacceptable and reckless.

Finally, I want to make this clear: the House, under the leadership of Speaker Johnson, has voted to fully fund DHS five separate times. It is the Senate that has failed to do so – and not because the majority of the Senate doesn’t favor it. In fact, the majority of both chambers have voted to fund the Department of Homeland Security repeatedly. The hold up during this time of threats to our nation is all because of the misuse of a Senate rule, the filibuster. This is an issue I will delve into deeper during a later column.

So, what do we, as a nation, do now? In this moment, we should correct dangerous political rhetoric, move to immediately fund the agencies that keep us safe, and unite as a nation. We must not allow these types of horrific attacks to persist. As President Trump said in his statement after the assassination attempt in Butler, we must “show our True Character as Americans, remaining Strong and Determined.”

The United States of America is the greatest country this Earth has ever known. We must not allow evil from within to undermine our traditions of peaceful dissent and respect for those who hold opposing political views. Surely that is something that all Americans, regardless of party, can accept, celebrate, and practice when engaged in political debate and discussion.

My thoughts and prayers are with the President, my colleagues, and everyone who was put in danger at the White House Corespondents dinner tonight. Thank you to the Secret Service and law enforcement for their swift and brave action. Political violence is never acceptable.

This week, I continued working through the appropriations process while meeting with South Texas leaders, advocates, and constituents on issues important to our communities.

During a hearing with the Secretary of Veterans Affairs, I discussed the future of the new Audie L. Murphy VA Medical Center in San Antonio and the expansion/construction of the new Laredo VA Clinic to expand capacity and improve access to care for veterans across South Texas.

As part of the Energy and Water Appropriations process, I helped secure $5.5 million for the Southwest Border Regional Commission and continued efforts to move the Chacon Creek project forward in Laredo. I also supported the bipartisan 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act to help increase housing supply and bring down housing costs for working families.

I also welcomed several visitors from Hidalgo County and across the Rio Grande Valley, including representatives from LUPE, VIDA, local leaders, and community advocates. In addition, I spent time with the Texas Farm Bureau to talk about the importance of the Farm Bill and issues impacting farmers, ranchers, and rural communities across our state.

Cross-border trade and commerce are critical to the economy of South Texas and communities on both sides of the border.

I had the opportunity to talk with Sergio Fernando Gomez Lora, CEO of @cceoficialmx, to talk about the economic relationship between the United States and Mexico and the importance of continued cooperation between our private sectors.

In #TX28, we see firsthand how closely connected our economies are. From supply chains and workforce stability to manufacturing, agriculture, and trade, decisions made on either side of the border have a direct impact on jobs and businesses in our region.

We also talked about ways to strengthen economic coordination and keep commerce moving efficiently through our ports of entry.

I appreciated the conversation and look forward to continuing to work on issues important to the U.S.-Mexico economic partnership.

During today's Military Construction, Veterans Affairs, and Related Agencies budget hearing, I asked Secretary Doug Collins and Assistant Secretary Richard F. Topping about two priorities that matter deeply to South Texas veterans: a new Audie Murphy VA hospital in San Antonio and the expansion/construction of a new Laredo VA Clinic.

At Audie Murphy, we talked about keeping the project moving through environmental review and land acquisition so we can build the modern hospital our veterans deserve. San Antonio carries the proud title of Military City USA and veterans from across South Texas rely on Audie Murphy for specialized care every single day. The current hospital opened in the 1970s. Texas has grown. The veteran population has grown. The need for modern facilities has grown right alongside it. Secretary Collins reaffirmed the VA’s commitment to keep working with Congress and our local partners to move this project forward. I thank local leaders like Richard Perez for helping to move this new hospital forward.

We also discussed the future of the new Laredo VA Clinic. Years ago, I worked to secure the clinic because veterans along the border should not have to drive hours for care. Today, more veterans and military families call South Texas home and that clinic must keep pace with the community it serves. I appreciated the Department’s commitment to continue evaluating the facility’s needs and future expansion opportunities for Webb County and surrounding areas. 

I want to thank Secretary Collins, Assistant Secretary Topping, and our community partners for continuing to work with us. In Texas, we keep our word. Our veterans served this country with honor and I’ll keep fighting to make sure they receive the care and facilities they earned.

Recognizing the security challenges and economic opportunities in the Arctic and the High North, the Arctic Allies met to discuss our efforts to build a secure and prosperous region.

The Arctic is quickly becoming a sphere of increasing geopolitical strategic importance.  With Russia’s increased military activity and China’s growing strategic interest, we seek to bolster stability in the Arctic region.

We support NATO’s increased presence in the region through activities such as Arctic Sentry, Air Policing in Iceland, and Forward Land Forces Finland, as well as the ongoing strengthening of the Joint Forces Command in Norfolk, a new CAOC in Norway and the ongoing modernization of NORAD.

We also recognize the importance of economic and resource development in the Arctic and have tasked our experts to coordinate more closely on these issues, including research security, investment screening, and critical infrastructure modernization and protection.

We look forward to continuing to work together to achieve our common goal of a secure, prosperous, and peaceful Arctic.

Birth rates are low, and too few homes are being built. Housing policy demonstrates the idea of the laboratory of democracy.

States may try novel social and economic experiments without risk to the rest of the country.

Each week, we share stories of those whose service strengthens the fabric of our community. This week, we remember and honor a dear friend, trusted partner, and visionary leader—Linda Salley of Levittown, whom we sadly lost last week.

Linda was one of our first Hometown Heroes, and for good reason. There are some people whose work does more than serve a community. It enlarges it, deepens its memory, and leaves behind a light by which others may find their way.

Linda was such a person.

A gifted educator, lifelong learner, and devoted woman of faith, Linda dedicated her life to the belief that every person carries a story worthy of being heard. As a founding member, President, and Executive Director of the African American Museum of Bucks County, she preserved, illuminated, and celebrated Bucks County’s rich African American history, culture, and legacy.

For years, under Linda’s extraordinary leadership, the museum carried its mission across our region—into schools, museums, churches, civic spaces, and community gatherings—bringing stories too often left untold into the light.

I have been deeply honored to work alongside Linda over the years and see firsthand the depth of her conviction and the power of her vision. One of the great honors of my service has been helping Linda and the African American Museum of Bucks County secure a permanent home at historic Boone Farm in Middletown Township.

For Linda, Boone Farm was never just a location. It was the fulfillment of a promise: that the history she worked so faithfully to preserve would finally have a place to stand, a place to teach, and a place to endure.

Long after today, children will walk through those doors. Families will see themselves in the story. Neighbors will learn, remember, and understand. And in that sacred work of memory, Linda’s hand will still be guiding us.

For the all she preserved, the countless lives she touched, and the light she leaves behind, Linda Salley will forever be a Hometown Hero.

Since the administration dragged us into a war with Iran, gas prices have exploded. Every commute costs more. Every school run costs more. Every small business running on tight margins is bleeding cash to fill the tank.

So here’s one thing we’re doing about it.

I’m cosponsoring the Gas Prices Relief Act, introduced by Rep. Chris Pappas and led in the Senate by Senator Mark Kelly. Here’s what you need to know about the bill, and why the fine print matters.

Immediate relief. We suspend the entire 18.4-cent federal gas tax through October 1, 2026. Those savings hit your wallet the next time you fill up.

Real enforcement. Some “tax holiday” proposals let oil companies quietly pocket the difference and call it a day. Not ours. We direct the Treasury to aggressively monitor the market and punish any producer that fails to pass the savings to you.

No tradeoffs on safety. Some reckless ideas floating around Washington would starve our roads and bridges of funding to pay for this. Ours doesn’t. We force the Treasury’s General Fund to reimburse the Highway Trust Fund dollar-for-dollar. Every local infrastructure project keeps moving.

Read the fine print on other plans. Politicians are suddenly racing to call for a gas tax suspension. A gas tax holiday without consumer protections is just a taxpayer-funded subsidy for Big Oil. A gas tax holiday without a Highway Trust Fund backfill is a disaster for the roads your family drives on every day.

This bill is an emergency cushion for families navigating a crisis they didn’t cause. I’ll keep fighting to force Washington to pass clean, fully protected relief, and to pass it now.

Fun Fact Friday: As we celebrate the 250th anniversary of American independence, I want to highlight some of the signers of the Declaration of Independence.
Robert Treat Paine was born in Boston, Massachusetts, in 1731. He served as a chaplain during the French and Indian War. He later moved to Taunton, Massachusetts, where he lived and practiced law. After the Boston Massacre, Paine’s dedication to the Patriots’ cause began to grow. He was elected to the Continental Congress, where he participated in debates over independence, and was nicknamed the “Objection-Maker,” by Benjamin Rush. Paine later served as the Massachusetts Attorney General and a member of the Massachusetts Supreme Court. Paine signed the Declaration of Independence on August 2, 1776.

Trump folded on AI – here’s why that matters:

Artificial intelligence is moving fast. Faster than most people in Washington are prepared for.

It is already changing how people work, how companies operate, how our kids learn, and how countries compete.

Powerful, disruptive technology needs serious leadership.

That’s why President Trump’s decision to walk away from his own AI executive order this week is such a failure. Not because the order was perfect – it was not. From what has been reported, it would have created a voluntary process for government agencies to evaluate some frontier AI systems for risks and vulnerabilities before public release. I don’t think that goes nearly far enough for a technology changing this rapidly, but even that modest step was apparently too much once a few powerful tech executives pushed back.

That should bother everyone.

America cannot lead in AI if our policy is determined by whichever billionaire gets the President on the phone last. We need a strategy that supports innovation, protects workers, strengthens national security, and makes sure this technology benefits the country, not just a handful of big tech companies.

I have spent a lot of my life around advanced technology. In the Navy, at NASA, and now in the Senate, one thing is clear: when the stakes are high, you do not just hope everything works out. You test. You plan. You ask hard questions. You build safeguards. That is not anti-innovation. That is how serious people handle serious systems and innovate responsibly.

AI is going to shape the future of work, our energy grid, cybersecurity, and our competition with China. Getting this right matters for families in Arizona and across the country.

We should want American companies to lead the world. But we don't do that by prioritizing short-term company profits above all else. We need to make sure AI tools are deployed safely and responsibly.

The President had a chance to show that he understands that. Instead, when powerful billionaires got him on the phone, he backed down.

That is a failure.

We can do better than that. And we have seen why we can’t rely on the whims of a president to do that. To truly lead, Congress needs to get in the game with real, forward-looking policy on AI.

Larry Harper, a resident of Hollister, brings 35 years of experience as a certified peer support specialist and licensed minister to his work helping individuals and families find hope, healing, and a path forward. Since making eastern North Carolina home 8 years ago, Harper has used his lived experience in recovery to support those facing addiction, mental health challenges, and life’s most difficult moments.

As the founder of H.O.P.E. — Helping Our People Escape — Harper has created one of the few recovery support resources available in the Hollister community. Through faith-based recovery meetings, mentorship, and outreach, he provides individuals struggling with addiction a supportive environment centered on healing, accountability, and second chances. His work also extends to Warren Correctional Institution and Freedom House Recovery Center, where he encourages individuals on their journey toward sobriety and stability.

We are proud to recognize Larry Harper for his unwavering commitment to helping others overcome addiction, restore hope, and build stronger futures across eastern North Carolina.

On May 21st, 2026, the House voted on H.R. 1329, the Smithsonian American Women’s History Museum Act. This bill authorized a location on the National Mall for the building of the American Women’s History Museum, which originated through funding by a Democrat controlled House in 2020 (although a location was never secured, keeping the building in limbo). While celebrating outstanding women who have contributed to our nation’s history is laudable, this authorizing legislation did little to stop the Museum’s already existing radical agenda, celebrating LGBT, climate, open borders, and abortion activism, as evidenced by the links below on their website. For this reason, my conscience led me to a “no” vote.

While I am glad that Rep. Mary Miller got language included in the bill to prohibit biological men from being displayed in the museum, it didn’t go far enough to stop the liberal agenda as the Smithsonian Women’s History Museum’s website is already promoting stories with activist titles such as “Learn More about LGBTQ+ Women with these Podcasts, Paintings, and Portraits,” “Exploring Border Stories with Artist Tanya Aguiñiga,” “How the Daughters of Bilitis Organized for Lesbian Rights,” and “LGBTQ+ Women Who Made History.” 

(https://womenshistory.si.edu/blog/learn-more-about-lgbtq-women-these-podcasts-paintings-and-portraits, https://womenshistory.si.edu/blog/exploring-border-stories-artist-tanya-aguiniga, https://womenshistory.si.edu/blog/how-daughters-bilitis-organized-lesbian-rights, and https://womenshistory.si.edu/blog/lgbtq-women-who-made-history)

Without clear statutory guardrails to protect against radical left-wing ideology being injected into American/women’s history at the Smithsonian, this new museum is set to provide a permanent venue on our National Mall for pro-abortion and LGBT ideology.

The United States just celebrated the 250th anniversary of our Founders dedicating America unto God and seeking pardon for the sins of our nation. I could not support a bill that would place a Smithsonian museum on the National Mall that advocates what the Bible defines as sexual immorality, as well as the killing of the unborn. I respect, but disagree with, those who supported the measure because they believed it’s the best change we could get.

R to @RepYassAnsari: And think about how this would actually work in practice, and I’ll use Iranians as an example.

Right now, more than 12,000 Iranian nationals who are here legally on student or work visas are already living in fear because of the Trump Administration’s USCIS processing pause. I recently introduced The Iranian Temporary Immigration Relief Act (H.R. 8740) with @RepTomSuozzi to grant Temporary Protected Status (TPS) and work authorization to eligible Iranian nationals.

It would impact people applying for green cards, many of whom have been living in the United States LEGALLY for years, building careers, raising American children, and creating full lives here.

That includes thousands of Iranians who studied in the U.S. and are now working as scientists, engineers, researchers, and doctors at top companies and hospitals across this country. I personally know people in these exact circumstances.

An Iranian married to an American citizen, with U.S. citizen children, could be forced to leave the country and process their case from abroad. But there is no U.S. embassy in Iran. And they could be sent back into the hands of a brutal regime in the middle of war and political repression.

Stephen Miller-the architect behind Trump’s mass deportation agenda-has always pushed cruel and extreme policies. But this is beyond the pale. The human cost will be catastrophic for families across this country.

They’ve been lying when they say they support immigration “the right way.” This radical policy will target people here LEGALLY, including people married to Americans and parents of U.S. citizen children.

It will separate families for months or even years, devastate communities, and kill jobs.

We have to do everything we can to stop this insanity.

H001100.text:
Major news for Western Colorado.

I am very happy to announce that the federal government is moving forward with approximately $40 million to help preserve the historic Shoshone water rights, one of the most important water protections on the Colorado River.

These flows are critical for Western Colorado agriculture, ranching, rural communities, recreation, and long-term water reliability across the Western Slope.

From the beginning, I made preservation of the Shoshone water rights a top priority and worked directly with the Department of the Interior, local water leaders, agricultural producers, and stakeholders across Colorado to help move this effort forward — including raising the importance of Shoshone directly with Secretary Burgum before the House Natural Resources Committee.

Water issues in the West require persistence, partnership, and practical solutions. This milestone reflects a great deal of hard work and collaboration from people across Colorado who stayed at the table and remained focused on getting this done.

I’ll continue working to ensure Western Colorado has a strong voice in the water decisions that shape our future. #CO03

Today, I chaired a House Indian and Insular Affairs Subcommittee hearing that included consideration of the Don Young–Doug LaMalfa Indian Buffalo Management Act.

This bipartisan legislation supports Tribal governments and organizations managing buffalo herds, restoring habitat, and expanding economic opportunities tied to buffalo stewardship. We also discussed the importance of reducing federal barriers that slow locally driven projects in Indian Country.

I appreciated Intertribal Buffalo Council President Ervin Carlson joining the hearing to testify and share his perspective on Tribal-led buffalo restoration efforts.
Buffalo remain deeply connected to the history, culture, and livelihoods of Tribal communities across the West, and Congress should continue supporting that stewardship for future generations. #CO03 🦬

I recently toured Orchard Mesa Irrigation District facilities and joined local water managers, ranchers, agricultural producers, Mesa County Commissioner Bobbie Daniel, and Colorado River Water Conservation District General Manager Andy Mueller for a water roundtable focused on drought conditions, irrigation operations, and the outlook for the growing season across the Western Slope. 

With low snowpack and dry conditions already impacting communities, these conversations are critical to understanding the challenges facing rural Colorado on the ground.

I’ll continue working to protect Western Colorado water interests, strengthen long-term water reliability, and ensure rural communities have a strong voice in the decisions shaping the future of the West. #CO03

Read more here: https://www.westernslopenow.com/news/western-slope-water-leaders-warn-of-drought-conditions-during-hurd-visit/

I recently joined Tribal leaders, conservation partners, and stakeholders to celebrate the 10th anniversary of the American buffalo being designated our national mammal.

I was proud to speak alongside Intertribal Buffalo Council President Ervin Carlson about the Don Young–Doug LaMalfa Indian Buffalo Management Act, legislation I introduced to support Tribal governments in restoring and managing buffalo herds and habitat.

The story of the buffalo is deeply tied to the history of Tribal nations and the American West. Tribal communities have led these stewardship efforts for generations, and Congress should be a partner in supporting that work for the future. #CO03 🦬

This week, I questioned Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum before the House Natural Resources Committee on issues that matter to communities across Western and Southern Colorado.

We discussed protecting Shoshone water rights, proactive wildfire mitigation, improving public safety coordination in Tribal communities, and stopping forced wolf reintroduction in Colorado.

These are real issues impacting rural communities, agriculture, public safety, and long term water reliability across #CO03. I’ll keep working to advance practical, locally driven solutions and make sure Western and Southern Colorado has a voice in these decisions.

Our office remains committed to working alongside local and federal partners to ensure the CNMI’s recovery needs continue to be heard and addressed.
